intervals.label: construction and installation
intervals.locator: INSPIRE experiment record 1110643, fields date_approved and date_completed
intervals.note: Mirrors experiment:lhcb's construction interval. Confidence is 'uncertain': experiment:lhcb's matching interval note explains why INSPIRE's date_completed field ('2008-09') should not be taken at face value for an active, non-terminal experiment (ATLAS's and LHCf's records show the placeholder '9999' in the same field).

end.note: Ends at the LHC-wide start of Long Shutdown 3 (June 2026); LHCb cannot record collisions the LHC is not delivering.

intervals.label: operating
intervals.note: The detector has recorded data (with the Upgrade I replacement of its tracking/trigger subsystems in 2019-2023) continuously since first collisions; see experiment:lhcb for the full run/shutdown history.

end.note: CERN schedule: the LHC resumes operation in mid-2030; the rest of the CERN complex restarts in stages from mid-2028.

intervals.label: Long Shutdown 3 / ECAL and RICH enhancements
intervals.locator: home.cern/science/long-shutdown-3, item of 5 August 2026 "The LHC is being warmed up from near absolute zero to room temperature"
intervals.note: The inner part of the electromagnetic calorimeter is replaced and the RICH electronics are upgraded during Long Shutdown 3. The bounds and the sources' wording are those of experiment:lhcb, whose interval note also records that the 2024 LHCb page gives older LS3 dates than CERN's mid-2030 schedule.
intervals.quote: The LHCb experiment will upgrade the inner part of the Electromagnetic Calorimeter and the electronics of the Ring Imaging Cherenkov detectors in the next LHC Long Shutdown (LS3).

name: LHCb detector
notes: Placed at site:cern-point-8-lhcb. The detector paper (2008 JINST 3 S08005) was found but its full text was blocked by CERN's document-server bot protection (cds.cern.ch) and exceeded the fetch size limit at the SISSA mirror; only its abstract (via the INSPIRE literature API) is cited. Pseudorapidity coverage, dipole bending power and the RICH/VELO/calorimeter/muon-system specs are left unsourced rather than guessed.
The detector record carries the same Long Shutdown 3 interval and status as experiment:lhcb, so that the two agree.

placements.locator: home.cern LHCb experiment page, paragraph beginning "The 5600-tonne LHCb detector"
placements.quote: sits 100 metres below ground near the town of Ferney-Voltaire, France

length.quote: It is 21 metres long, 10 metres high and 13 metres wide, and sits 100 metres below ground near the village of Ferney-Voltaire, France.

total_mass.note: CONFLICT: lhcb-outreach.web.cern.ch's own detector page gives '4,500 tonne'; see experiment:lhcb key_specs note. The 5600 t figure is used here for the same reason (independent corroboration with a verbatim quote from two sources).
total_mass.quote: The 5600-tonne LHCb detector is made up of a forward spectrometer and planar detectors.

summary.plain: The LHCb detector is a single forward-pointing spectrometer, 21 metres long, 5600 tonnes, sitting 100 metres underground at CERN. Instead of surrounding the collision point on all sides like ATLAS or CMS, it stacks its sub-detectors one behind another to catch particles thrown forward by the collision.
summary.technical: Single-arm forward spectrometer at LHC Point 8: VELO, dipole magnet, two RICH detectors, tracking stations, calorimeters and a muon system arranged sequentially along the outgoing beam direction over ~20 m; 5600 t (per INSPIRE/home.cern; lhcb-outreach states 4500 t, unresolved conflict), 21 m × 10 m × 13 m.

technology.quote: Instead of surrounding the entire collision point with an enclosed detector as do ATLAS and CMS, the LHCb experiment uses a series of subdetectors to detect mainly forward particles.
technology.value: single-arm forward spectrometer with a warm dipole magnet, vertex locator (VELO), two RICH detectors, tracking stations, calorimeters and a muon system
